messages.subject_clean: R Crashing in Yosemite OS X
messages.body_plain:
Has anyone else been having problems with R crashing on Yosemite OS X? It's starting to drive me crazy! I'm using the regular install of R and it works fine until I go to open an R document and then I get a blank open file window, a pinwheel, and the only remedy is to force quit. So it seems opening documents is what kills it the most reliably, although sometimes it just randomly crashes too.

If there's no fix, I'm considering using a text editor for code and copy/pasting to the console or using R in terminal, which I don't really want to have to do.

Also, I keep getting this error and google doesn't turn anything up: "2015-05-01 15:36:10.131 R[2813:39837] *** WARNING: Method convertPointFromBase: in class NSView is deprecated on 10.7 and later. It should not be used in new applications."

I don't know if that's a different question or if it's related.

Thanks for thoughts!

Mila

messages.body_plain:
Dear D-RUGgies,

I am having more issues with a map I'm making that I cannot figure out. Thanks to Ryan Peek who responded to my earlier plea for help.

The attached map shows the worldwide distribution of eelgrass (data from http://maps.iucnredlist.org/map.html?id=153538) and some sampling sites. My issues, which are visible in the map, are as follows:

1. The polygon is cut off near the International Date Line.

2. Some enclosed bodies of water (e.g. Mediterranean, Hudson Bay, Sea of Japan) are filled with color (potentially twice?) when I don't want them to be.

My code is below, and also attached. Please let me know if you can help me with these issues. Thanks in advance!

Much appreciated,

Matt

###### ZEN
### MAP OF SITES USING GGPLOT/GGMAP
# by Matt Whalen
# last updated 6 May 2015
library(ggmap)
library(sp)
library(rgeos)
library(maptools)
library(ggplot2)

## a nice world map
data(wrld_simpl)

### The following section is complements of stack exchange (http://gis.stackexchange.com/questions/79350/plotting-a-certain-range-in-azimuthal-projection-using-ggplot2)
# make a bounding box for the northern hemisphere
latlim = 22
g <- gridlines(wrld_simpl, easts=0, norths=latlim, ndiscr = 200)
x <- c(coordinates(g)[[1]][[1]][,1], rev(coordinates(g)[[1]][[1]][,1]), coordinates(g)[[1]][[1]][1])
y <- c(rep(90, 200), rep(latlim, 200), 90)
bnds <- cbind(x=x, y=y)
SP <- SpatialPolygons(list(Polygons(list(Polygon(bnds)), "1")), proj4string=CRS(proj4string(wrld_simpl)))
## end section

### The following section is courtesy of Roger Bivand https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-sig-geo/2012-June/015340.html
gI <- gIntersects(wrld_simpl, SP, byid=TRUE)
out <- vector(mode="list", length=length(which(gI)))
ii <- 1
for (i in seq(along=gI)) if (gI[i]) {
  out[[ii]] <- gIntersection(wrld_simpl[i,], SP)
  row.names(out[[ii]]) <- row.names(wrld_simpl)[i]; ii <- ii+1
}
out1 <- do.call("rbind", out)

# fortify SP object to plot wiht ggplot
mymap <- fortify(out1, region='id')
mymap <- mymap[order(mymap$order), ]
## end section

# Add shape file
library(rgdal)
setwd("C:\\Users\\Matt_Whalen\\Documents\\ZEN Project\\Map of Sites\\species_153538")
Zostera <- readOGR( ".", "species_153538")
Zostera <- spTransform(Zostera, CRS("+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84"))
Zostera <- fortify(Zostera)

# Sites
Sites <- c('AK','BB','BC','FI','JN','JS','MA','NC','NN','PO','QU','SD','SW','VA','WA')
Lats  <- c(59.648,38.317,49.000,60.100,43.060,34.178,42.426,34.683,67.233,36.997,49.113,32.714,58.314,37.217,46.500)
Longs <- c(-151.436,-123.033,-123.100,21.700,
          144.911-360,132.550-360,  # Note, Japanese site had to be adjusted by 360 degrees to work with "maps" package
          -70.919,-76.600,15.200,-7.829,-68.179,-117.226,
          11.548,-76.383,-124.000)  # Note, Quebec longitutide was listed as positive but should be negative...needs to be fixed in Supplementary Table

# Wrap Site info into a data.frame
SiteList <- data.frame( site=Sites, lat=Lats, long=Longs, cols=Cols, adjx=Adjx, adjy=Adjy )

# Make the dang map
ggplot(data=mymap,aes(x=long,y=lat,group=group)) +
     coord_map("azequidistant",orientation=c(90,0,270)) +
     geom_polygon(data=SP,fill='lightskyblue') +
     geom_polygon(aes(x=long, y=lat, group=group), fill='seagreen', size=.2,color='darkgreen',
                  data=Zostera, alpha=0.8) +
     geom_polygon(fill=gray(0.85)) +
     geom_path(color=gray(0.7),aes(x=long,y=lat),size=0.1) +
     geom_point(data=SiteList,aes(x=long, y=lat,group=NULL),size=3.5) +
     theme_bw() +
     theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA), panel.border=element_blank() ) +
     theme(axis.line=element_blank(),axis.text.x=element_blank(),axis.text.y=element_blank(),
           axis.ticks=element_blank(), axis.title.x=element_blank(), axis.title.y=element_blank() ) +
     theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

I haven't tested the code, but I think this should do it:

lapply(combn(ncol(x), 2, simplify=FALSE), function(i) cor(x[i][1], x[i][2]))

...where x is a data.frame with your 46 variables as columns and observations as rows.  You can then do a similar lapply with paste() as the function to generate names for the pairwise correlations.

Actually, cor() and cov() accept whole matrices or data.frames, so you could also do cor(x), where x is your whole data as a data.frame or matrix with variables as columns.  That is, there's no need for lapply, etc.

I don't know what to say about categorical/factor variables. I don't know of a good correlation measure for a continuous and a categorical variable.  I think cor(method="spearman") or cor(method="kendall") will run, but what the correlation value means in such cases is hard to interpret.

I would get a cor() value for all the paris of continuous variables, and then examine the relationship of each categorical variable to the rest of the data on its own.  For the latter you can use generalized pairs plots as implemented in the gpairs package and the ggpairs() function of the GGally package; they have many ways of plotting different kinds of data.  Another option is to use scagnostics (http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/scagnostics/index.html) to explore the relationship between each pair of variables.

summary(aov(SalmonRehang ~ Hatchery, data=XXX))

messages.body_plain:
as.Date(), by default tries to convert dates assuming their format is Y/M/D. That’s why this sometimes works but badly - “9/9/13”, is interpreted as September 13, 0009, as opposed to September 9, 2013. With a date like “11/27/13”, it fails, because there is no month 27. Since ALL the HatchDate column values fail, it returns an error, but for the other columns it just returns NA.

So you need to do as Brandon suggested: put a format="%m/%d/%y" argument into each of your as.Date() calls.

The shorthand codes for date formats can all be found in ?strptime, and Bonnie’s tutorial also goes into some detail on how the lubridate package has some convenience functions for this.
​

Hi Laura,

Since it doesn't make sense to take a correlation of categorial variables (e.g. factors in R), you need to remove these columns before the correlation calculation. You can do this with (using iris as an example):

Similar to your problem:

> cor(iris)
Error in cor(iris) : 'x' must be numeric

A solution

> cor(iris[, sapply(iris, is.numeric)])
             Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
Sepal.Length    1.0000000  -0.1175698    0.8717538   0.8179411
Sepal.Width    -0.1175698   1.0000000   -0.4284401  -0.3661259
Petal.Length    0.8717538  -0.4284401    1.0000000   0.9628654
Petal.Width     0.8179411  -0.3661259    0.9628654   1.0000000

I think I and other DRUG folks are happy to keep helping with these small questions, but for your long term sanity I would recommend you learn a bit more about R data types and structures. This will help you reason through tiny problems and not be continually frustrated by the numerous data type/structure issues that will pop up as you use R. I find that teaching beginners about R data types and structures is enough to allow them to solve 80% of their issues on their own.

For example, why sapply() works with the dataframe iris above only makes sense if you realize dataframes are just lists of columns (and sapply iterates through each list element — a column — and asks if it's a numeric object). Issues like type coercion and recycling are also very important to understand so you don't get unexpected results.

"R in a Nutshell" has a quick tutorial on this, and is available online through the UC Davis campus proxy on Safari Books. UC Davis's own Norman Matloff's "The Art of R Programming" is also quite good.

hope this helps,
Vince

messages.subject: Friday: Qualitative Text Analysis in R using RDQA
messages.subject_clean: Friday: Qualitative Text Analysis in R using RDQA
messages.body_plain:
[To those on this list in the social sciences and humanities: Please forward this announcement to your grad group/departmental listservs or other groups that may be interested in qualitative text analysis.]

Hi all,

This Friday at the Davis R Users Group <http://www.noamross.net/davis-r-users-group.html>, Mallory Johnson will give a presentation on doing qualitative text analysis in R using RDQA. From Mallory:
>
> R is most often associated with quantitative analysis, but the platform is also useful for qualitative research. Friday’s presentation will introduce the R package for Qualitative Data Analysis (RQDA), a qualitative analysis software that resides within the frame of R. RQDA’s simple to use GUI makes organizing and analyzing textual data easy. Use it for organizing field notes, theory building, or even literature reviews— any time you need to search for keywords, themes, or references across multiple text files.

Per usual, the presentation + Q&A will run from 10-11 in Wickson 2124, and we will have open co-work time from 11-12. Webcast info to come, and materials from the talk will be available on the blog afterwards.

Best,

Noam Ross

Hi Jens,

In case this is an X-Y problem <http://mywiki.wooledge.org/XyProblem>  — why do you need to copy and paste data from RStudio to a spreadsheet? My (maybe too opinionated) view is that this probably shouldn't be happening — shuffling data to and from R with copy/paste is a recipe for different data versions to confound results (I've been bitten by something similar before).

The workflow I recommend to folks is: treat data as read only, meaning don't edit the data in a non-reproducible way. This way one set of data is tied to one set of results, and one set of code that produced those results. If you need to make changes in the data in the spreadsheet (e.g. if you made a data entry here), do that, save the results, and make a note of the changes (placing tabular data in version control is very useful here too). In my workflows, I have a raw data file (never changed), a cleaned data file (changed with Python or other scripting languages — spreadsheet changes can be made too), and then my R code reads the cleaned data file to run analyses and generate results. It may be different for your particular workflow though.

hope this helps,
Vince

read.excel <- function(header=TRUE,...) {
  read.table("clipboard",sep="\t",header=header,...)

messages.body_plain:
read.cb() and write.cb() in the Kmisc package actually do pretty much exactly this, but detect your operating system. e.g.,
read.cb <- function(sep='\t', header=TRUE, ...) {
  sn <- Sys.info()["sysname"]
  if (sn == "Darwin") {
    read.table( pipe("pbpaste"), header=header, sep=sep, ... )
  } else if (sn == "Windows") {
    read.table( "clipboard", header=header, sep=sep, ... )
  } else {
    stop("Reading from the clipboard is not implemented for your system (",
      sn, ") in this package.")
  }
}

cat.cb() and scan.cb() do the same thing for character data.
​

psplot <- ggplot(data, aes(x = p, color = flex2, fill = flex2)) + geom_density(alpha=.2) +
  ylab("Density") + xlab("Propensity Scores")

Thanks for your help.

If I understand you correctly — the issue here is in interpretation. The y-axis of a density curve (as long as it's not cumulative density) is not a probability, so does not need to be less than or equal to 1. Rather, the probability is the integral between an interval on the x-axis, which is the area under this curve. This post helps explain this in more depth: http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/4220/a-probability-distribution-value-exceeding-1-is-ok

HTH,
V
